item.title: Mismatch Negativity and General Cognitive Ability - A Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Intelligence or general cognitive ability (GCA) is fundamental to human behavior and cognition. It impacts important life outcomes like educational success, and even health and longevity have been related to differences in GCA. Understanding the biological basis of such individual variations presents a crucial goal of neuroscience. The mismatch negativity (MMN) is an event-related brain potential that can be measured when-within a series of frequent standard stimuli, rare deviants are presented-and is suggested to reflect conscious (active) or unconscious (passive) detection processes of the brain. Importantly, variations in MMN amplitude and latency have been linked to differences in GCA. Yet findings vary considerably. This preregistered meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the current state of research. Following the study selection process in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, and the rating of study design quality with the Study Design and Implementation Assessment Device for Individual Difference Research (DIAD-ID), the association between GCA and MMN amplitude and latency was examined in 645 healthy adults across 12 included studies. The estimated across-sample associations between MMN and GCA were small, but significant (MMN amplitude-GCA: r = -0.09, MMN latency-GCA: r = -0.16; p < 0.01) and moderators were identified. Between-sample heterogeneity was moderate, with no evidence of publication bias. Our findings suggest that higher cognitive ability is associated with slightly stronger and faster MMN responses. However, the low estimated across-sample effect sizes and the small number of included studies also highlight the need for more research.

item.title: Where could the brain keep a symbol?
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Neuroscience routinely describes memories as stored neural symbols, yet durable memory and successful retrieval do not establish a separately accessible symbolic vehicle. I distinguish retention, the claim that a physical change persists and later influences behavior, from symbolic storage, the stronger computational claim that a description can be accessed independently of the operation it specifies. The criterion is functional and system-relative and does not rule out neural activity as access. It requires specifying, before testing, the candidate vehicle, its proposed use, the system boundary, and an endogenous route reaching the vehicle without using it. DNA meets the criterion: replication preserves nucleotide sequence without producing the encoded gene product. Evidence from synapses and circuits establishes persistent, functionally useful organization but has not shown this separation for any neural memory vehicle; in these states, identified reads are executions that modify what they read. Hippocampal replay, neuromodulation, and artificial-network checkpoints show that the verdict depends on the vehicle and operations compared. I agree with Gallistel that intracellular nucleic acid mechanisms could provide a genuine store, but disagree that behavioral precision alone requires one. Maintained coupling, in which memory is sustained by continual recalibration rather than read from a store, offers an alternative whose predictions depend on error source: drift can be corrected where a reference signal remains, but a unique, never-revisited episode offers none. Current evidence favors retention without symbolic storage in synapses and circuits; I propose operational tests that could overturn this verdict. Either way, retention and use remain memory.

item.title: Pre-stimulus cortical state predicts behavioral performance differently across distractor-learning contexts.
item.description:
Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
Performance during distractor-laden visual search may vary with learned attentional settings and ongoing brain state. We reanalyzed an fMRI visual-search dataset (N = 34) to test whether pre-stimulus global signal (GS), a broad state-sensitive BOLD measure, predicts subsequent performance and cortical responsivity across two distractor-learning groups. Participants searched for an orientation target while ignoring (same-dimension) orientation or (different-dimension) color distractors. The spatially biased, more frequent distractor dimension was orientation in one group and color in the other; so, the groups differed in both spatial regularity and relative exposure to each dimension. Same-dimension distractors produced strong behavioral interference and recruited Dorsal Attention and Salience/Ventral Attention networks, whereas different-dimension distractors produced little interference. Spatial learning was also more robust when regularity applied to the target-relevant same dimension. Pre-stimulus GS predicted response speed in opposite directions across groups: higher GS preceded slower responses in the same-dimension spatial-bias group, but faster responses in the different-dimension spatial-bias group. Pre-stimulus Default-Mode Network activity showed a convergent group-dependent pattern. Higher pre-stimulus GS generally preceded reduced activity in Dorsal Attention, Salience/Ventral Attention, Control, Early Visual, and Default Mode regions. Exploratory analyses suggested that associations between neural attenuation and the GS-performance relationship varied by group, particularly on different-dimension trials. Together, these findings reveal the relationship between pre-stimulus cortical state and subsequent attentional performance to differ across distractor-learning contexts, even though GS-related cortical attenuation is largely context-general.

item.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels.
item.description:
eLife
Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse's contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

item.title: Aperiodic EEG Activity Is a Domain-Specific Marker of Attentional Aging in Neurotypical Adults.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Aperiodic neural activity has been reliably shown to be reduced among older adults, and these reductions are associated with age-related cognitive decline. These results suggest that aperiodic activity, as measured by the spectral exponent, might be a viable electrophysiological biomarker for cognitive aging. However, this has not been tested longitudinally, within participants, during normal aging. Here, we used a longitudinal cohort of either sex to test whether changes in aperiodic activity between two sessions, ∼5 years apart, track behavioral change across two domains: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Test) and executive function (modified Simon task). We found that aperiodic activity declined within individuals after the interval, independent of age at baseline. This within-person change tracked concurrent changes in reaction times during sustained attention but was not associated with changes in any Simon task measure. Within a resampling framework, the aperiodic-PVT association was stable across cohort resamples and independently fitted partitions, though it was not confirmed in a small, frozen held-out set. These findings suggest the longitudinal decline in aperiodic activity tracks attentional processing speed rather than executive function, supporting its potential as a domain-specific biomarker of attentional aging in neurotypical populations.

item.title: Probing the Neural Geometry of Conscious Object Perception in Time.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. In contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level.

item.title: Perception of Tones versus Tone Streams under Random Multi-tone Masking and Its Representation in Auditory Cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream.

item.title: Representation of Emotional Expressions across the Face and Voice Brain Networks.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is fundamental to successful social interaction, yet how the brain represents emotional information across sensory systems remains unclear. Here, we systematically mapped the contribution of individually defined face- and voice-selective cortical regions in 24 human participants of either sex to unimodal and crossmodal emotion expressions. Using multivariate pattern classification, we show that emotional expressions are robustly decodable from the dominant sensory modality across all individually defined face- and voice-selective areas and that these representations cannot be accounted for by low- and mid-level stimulus properties alone. Strikingly, emotional information from the nondominant modality-vocal expressions within face networks and facial expressions within voice networks-was also represented throughout the network, with the exception of the occipital face areas. Crossmodal decoding further revealed a shared neural code for facial and vocal emotions in the temporal voice areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus, indicating that these regions contain emotion representations that generalize across sensory modalities. Furthermore, in most face- and voice-selective regions, audiovisual emotional expressions could be distinguished from representations elicited by the dominant unimodal modality, indicating that bimodal signals are not simply represented as their strongest sensory component. Together, these findings reveal that emotion representations are distributed broadly across face- and voice-selective regions and identify temporofrontal regions as key sites supporting modality-independent emotion representations.

item.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Functions in Patients With Essential Tremor Without Dementia: Beyond the Cerebellum.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Essential tremor (ET) is characterized not only by motor disturbances but also, in many cases, by a wide array of cognitive symptoms. Accumulating evidence implicates pathways beyond the cerebellum by which cognitive changes emerge. However, the extracerebellar neuropathologic correlates of specific cognitive symptoms have not been examined. This study evaluated these potential clinicopathologic associations in older adults with ET. Methods Participants were adults ≥55 years with ET who were followed prospectively and longitudinally and donated their brains for neuropathologic evaluation as part of the Clinical-Pathological Study of Cognitive Impairment in Essential Tremor study. Cognitive outcomes included attention, executive function, language, memory, and visuospatial function. Postmortem neuropathologic assessment included Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) neuritic plaque scores, Thal β-amyloid A score, Braak and Braak neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) stage, and Braak Lewy pathology stage. Regional cerebral cortical atrophy ratings (neocortical and hippocampal), cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and markers of cerebrovascular health were also rated. Regression models examined neuropathologic correlates of cognitive function, adjusting for numerous confounders. Sensitivity analyses examined robustness of findings. Results The sample consisted of 57 individuals with ET and without dementia (mean age = 88.6 ± 5.4 years; 54.4% female, 71.9% cognitively normal, 28.1% with mild cognitive impairment). Higher amyloid burden was associated with lower attention (CERAD β = -0.48, p < 0.001; Thal β = -0.37, p < 0.01) and lower executive function (CERAD β = -0.40, p 0.01; Thal β = -0.33, p = 0.01). CERAD score was associated with lower language (β = -0.31, p = 0.04). Braak NFT stage was associated with lower attention (β = -0.26, p = 0.04) and lower executive function (β = -0.28, p = 0.03). Hippocampal atrophy was associated with lower memory performance (β = -0.29, p = 0.04). Discussion Core pathologies of AD, amyloid and tau, are associated with decrements in attention and executive function in older adults with ET and without dementia, while hippocampal atrophy is associated with lower memory performance. These results, consistent with a growing literature on extracerebellar pathologies in ET, suggest that multidomain cognitive symptoms among older adults with ET and without dementia may be driven in large part by AD-related cortical degenerative processes. Ongoing work is examining the molecular basis of these processes. Limitations include a highly educated, demographically homogeneous, and relatively small sample, as well as a lack of a control group.

item.title: Nonconscious Multisensory Integration in the Ventriloquist Effect.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
The degree to which information from distinct sensory modalities can interact in the absence of conscious awareness remains controversial. The ventriloquist effect is a classical multisensory integration phenomenon that refers to the misperception of sound location toward concurrent visual stimulation, such as perceiving the voice of a ventriloquist actor as coming from the moving dummy. Here, we used metacontrast masking to render a brief flash stimulus nonconscious while 30 participants performed a sound localization task. We found that, despite being subjectively invisible and at chance at discriminating the flash location, participants were nevertheless biased to localize sounds toward the unconscious flash locations. The effect was present in virtually all participants, was nearly as large as the effect on conscious trials, and was robust to controls for individual differences in task performance. Decoding and ERP analyses of concurrently recorded EEG signals showed that the nonconscious flash location information was present until around 220 msec but not thereafter, suggesting that the visual influence on sound perception may have occurred before conscious broadcast. In support of this, early decoding accuracy on nonconscious trials predicted individual variation in the size of the unconscious ventriloquist effect. Our findings suggest that subjective perception is not required for the integration of signals originating in distinct sensory modalities prompting new questions about the role of subjective perception in multisensory integration.

item.title: Current Topics in the Encephalographic Study of Visual Attention.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
An enduring topic of scientific interest since the beginning of cognitive psychological research is visual attention. This phenomenon describes the process by which certain visual percepts are prioritized for deeper processing in the brain, while others receive reduced processing and thereby exert less influence on perception and behavior. In our daily lives, visual attention is critical to performance across countless situations-from navigating busy traffic to maintaining focus on a friend in a crowded room. Therefore, understanding the neural mechanisms that dictate how we select relevant visual information and filter out distractions is central to understanding one of the brain's most fundamental cognitive abilities. Because these attentional processes unravel rapidly in time and are reflected in dynamic patterns of cortical activity, encephalographic measures (i.e., electro- and magneto-encephalography) have been popular tools for their study. In 2025, attention researchers from across Europe gathered in Amsterdam for 2 days of meetings, discussion, and debate on current issues and future avenues in the encephalographic investigation of attention. This perspective piece distills the ideas and topics that emerged from that meeting into a field guide to contemporary encephalographic research on visual attention. It provides a partial snapshot of several ongoing research fields related to the study of visual attention, highlights where they are heading, and highlights which questions are likely to shape their future. We hope that this piece will be especially useful for early career researchers looking to enter the field but unsure about what their next research question should be.
